reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD & ACG
clinicalPearls: The great majority arise in a background of cirrhosis or chronic liver disease, most often from chronic hepatitis B or C, alcohol-related liver disease, or metabolic (fatty) liver disease
Chronic hepatitis B can cause HCC even without established cirrhosis because of the virus's direct oncogenic effect
Surveillance of at-risk patients with periodic ultrasound (with or without alpha-fetoprotein) allows detection at an earlier, treatable stage
Diagnosis can often be made non-invasively on multiphase CT or MRI when a nodule shows the characteristic arterial-phase enhancement with portal/delayed venous washout in a cirrhotic liver
Alpha-fetoprotein supports the diagnosis and aids monitoring but is neither sufficiently sensitive nor specific to be used alone
Prognosis and treatment depend jointly on tumour burden, vascular invasion or spread, and the degree of underlying liver dysfunction, so staging systems incorporate liver function
Curative options for early disease include surgical resection, liver transplantation, and local ablation, while transarterial and systemic therapies are used for more advanced stages
New or worsening decompensation in a cirrhotic patient, such as sudden ascites or a bloody effusion, should prompt urgent evaluation for HCC and possible tumour rupture or vascular invasion
Portal vein tumour thrombus is an important adverse feature that changes staging and management
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatocellular carcinoma develops through chronic hepatocyte injury, inflammation, and regeneration, which over years produces cirrhosis and accumulating genetic and epigenetic damage. Dysplastic nodules progress to frank carcinoma. As tumours grow they recruit an arterial blood supply distinct from the normal portal-dominant hepatic perfusion, which underlies the arterial hyperenhancement and venous washout seen on imaging. The tumour tends to invade the portal and hepatic veins, promoting intrahepatic spread and portal vein thrombosis, and can metastasise to lung, bone, and lymph nodes. Chronic hepatitis B additionally drives carcinogenesis through viral DNA integration and direct oncogenic proteins, sometimes producing cancer in a non-cirrhotic liver.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic liver disease from another primary
Regenerative or dysplastic nodule in cirrhosis
Focal nodular hyperplasia or hepatic adenoma
additionalInvestigations: Multiphase contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to assess enhancement pattern, tumour extent, and vascular invasion
Serum alpha-fetoprotein as an adjunct to diagnosis and for monitoring
Assessment of liver function and cirrhosis severity (e.g. Child-Pugh grading and portal hypertension)
Image-guided biopsy in selected cases where imaging is indeterminate
Staging for extrahepatic spread including chest imaging
redFlags: New decompensation in a cirrhotic patient (rapid ascites, jaundice, or variceal bleeding) suggesting HCC or vascular invasion
Sudden severe abdominal pain with haemodynamic instability indicating tumour rupture and haemoperitoneum
Portal or hepatic vein tumour thrombus indicating advanced disease
Bloody ascitic fluid or a rapidly enlarging liver mass
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on stage and residual liver function. Early tumours treated with resection, transplantation, or ablation can achieve long-term survival, whereas advanced disease with vascular invasion, extrahepatic spread, or poor liver function has a poor prognosis. Underlying cirrhosis independently limits life expectancy and treatment options.
pitfalls: Failing to enrol at-risk cirrhotic and chronic hepatitis B patients in surveillance, leading to late diagnosis
Relying on alpha-fetoprotein alone, which can be normal in HCC or raised in benign liver disease
Overlooking underlying liver dysfunction when planning aggressive treatment
Missing portal vein tumour thrombus, which alters staging and precludes some curative options
management: Treat early-stage tumours with curative intent by surgical resection, liver transplantation within accepted criteria, or local ablation such as radiofrequency or microwave ablation
Manage intermediate, liver-confined disease with transarterial chemoembolisation or radioembolisation
Treat advanced disease with systemic therapy, first-line combination immunotherapy such as atezolizumab with bevacizumab, or a tyrosine kinase inhibitor such as sorafenib or lenvatinib
Treat the underlying liver disease with antiviral therapy for hepatitis B or C and alcohol abstinence, and manage portal hypertension and decompensation
Choose treatment according to tumour burden, vascular invasion, and liver function, reassessing as the underlying cirrhosis evolves
Continue surveillance imaging with alpha-fetoprotein for new lesions and monitor treatment response
Coordinate care through a hepatobiliary multidisciplinary team and integrate palliative care in advanced disease
